explanation: Recognizing false labor helps avoid admitting mothers to the ward too early, which keeps them comfortable and reduces hospital overcrowding. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T2#BMP212_U2_T2_h1)

question: Where do true labor contractions often start before spreading to the front?

options.A: The lower extremities
options.B: The lower back
options.C: The right shoulder blade
options.D: The upper shoulders

explanation: True labor pain commonly starts in the lower back and wraps around toward the front of the abdomen. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T2#BMP212_U2_T2_h2)

question: A pregnant woman walks around for an hour, and her contractions become stronger and closer together. What does this suggest?

options.A: Dehydration because activity causes muscle cramps
options.B: False labor because movement always stops contractions
options.C: Braxton Hicks because walking makes them stronger
options.D: True labor because walking does not stop them

explanation: True labor contractions continue and grow stronger even when the mother walks around or changes position. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T2#BMP212_U2_T2_h2)

question: What is the common term for false labor contractions?

options.A: Placental detachment waves
options.B: Oxytocin surge cramps
options.C: Braxton Hicks contractions
options.D: Myometrial rupture spasms

explanation: False labor contractions are widely known as Braxton Hicks contractions. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T2#BMP212_U2_T2_h3)

question: How do false labor contractions usually react to rest or walking?

options.A: They turn into active second stage pushing
options.B: They immediately cause the cervix to open
options.C: They become much stronger and longer
options.D: They usually stop or slow down

explanation: Unlike true labor, false labor contractions are irregular and tend to fade away when the mother rests or changes her activity. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T2#BMP212_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is the most reliable sign that true labor has started?

options.A: A sudden increase in appetite
options.B: Progressive cervical change
options.C: Frequent maternal mood swings
options.D: Mild swelling in the ankles

explanation: The clearest sign of true labor is when the cervix thins and opens over time. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T2#BMP212_U2_T2_h4)

question: What does passing the bloody show mean in late pregnancy?

options.A: The cervix is softening and opening
options.B: The baby has turned into breech position
options.C: The amniotic fluid is fully infected
options.D: The placenta has completely detached

explanation: The bloody show is the mucus plug mixed with a small amount of blood, which is released as the cervix begins to open. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T2#BMP212_U2_T2_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT part of the initial midwife assessment for a woman who might be in labor?

options.A: Surgically repairing the perineum
options.B: Evaluating contraction patterns
options.C: Assessing maternal vital signs
options.D: Checking fetal heart tones

explanation: Perineal repair is done after the baby is born, not during the first assessment of someone who may be in labor. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T2#BMP212_U2_T2_h5)

question: A woman arrives at the clinic with irregular contractions and a closed, unchanged cervix. What is the best midwifery action?

options.A: Administer high-dose oxytocin drip to speed up the process
options.B: Immediately admit her to the labor ward for surgical induction
options.C: Reassure her, explain it is false labor, and send her home with guidance
options.D: Perform an emergency caesarean section because of the pain

explanation: When the cervix is closed and contractions are irregular, hospital admission is not needed, and the mother can be supported with advice at home. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T2#BMP212_U2_T2_h5)

question: At what cervical dilatation is the first stage of labor considered complete?

options.A: Six centimeters
options.B: Eight centimeters
options.C: Twelve centimeters
options.D: Ten centimeters

explanation: The first stage of labor spans from true labor onset until the cervix reaches full dilatation, which is measured as ten centimeters. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why must the upper part of the uterus contract while the lower part stays relaxed during labor?

options.A: To push the fetus downward while pulling the cervix open
options.B: To prevent the placenta from detaching too early in labor
options.C: To keep the amniotic fluid enclosed inside the lower segment
options.D: To stop maternal blood pressure from dropping during contractions

explanation: Active contraction of the upper segment generates the force needed to push the baby down, while the passive lower segment and cervix stretch to allow passage. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h1)

question: Which specific protein builds up in the uterine muscle to help electrical impulses spread across the whole uterus?

options.A: Hemoglobin
options.B: Albumin
options.C: Fibrinogen
options.D: Connexin-43

explanation: Connexin-43 forms gap junctions that connect myometrial cells electrically so the uterus can contract together as a single unit. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h2)

question: What is the main job of calcium inside uterine muscle cells during a contraction?

options.A: To keep the resting membrane potential stable and prevent cramps
options.B: To seal the gap junctions and stop the spread of signals
options.C: To activate enzymes that cause the muscle fibers to shorten
options.D: To relax the muscle fibers by blocking electrical impulses

explanation: A surge in intracellular calcium triggers the chemical signals required for the uterine muscle fibers to shorten and contract effectively. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h2)

question: What is the term for the ability of uterine muscle fibers to stay partly shortened after each contraction?

options.A: Polarity
options.B: Dilatation
options.C: Retraction
options.D: Hypertonia

explanation: Retraction is the progressive shortening of uterine muscle fibers during labor, which gradually pulls the cervix upward and prevents the baby from slipping back up. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h3)

question: What does fundal dominance mean during normal labor?

options.A: The cervix contracts harder than the rest of the uterine wall
options.B: Uterine activity only happens during the second stage of labor
options.C: Contractions are strongest and last longest at the top of the uterus
options.D: The lower uterine segment does most of the pushing work

explanation: Fundal dominance ensures that the main pushing force is directed downward from the top of the uterus toward the birth canal. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h3)

question: Which structural protein makes up most of a non-pregnant cervix?

options.A: Myosin
options.B: Collagen
options.C: Elastin
options.D: Keratin

explanation: Collagen provides the tough, fibrous support that keeps the cervix firm and closed throughout pregnancy. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which hormone keeps the cervix firm and tightly closed during most of pregnancy?

options.A: Prolactin
options.B: Progesterone
options.C: Estrogen
options.D: Oxytocin

explanation: Progesterone dominance throughout pregnancy keeps the cervix firm and suppresses ripening until labor is near. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h4)

question: What term describes the process of the cervix thinning and shortening before birth?

options.A: Lightning
options.B: Involuting
options.C: Engagement
options.D: Effacement

explanation: Effacement refers to the gradual softening, shortening, and thinning of the cervix before and during early labor. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h5)

question: How do cervical changes usually differ between a first-time mother and a woman who has given birth before?

options.A: First-time mothers dilate twice as fast as women who have given birth before
options.B: Multiparas have zero changes in cervical length until pushing begins
options.C: First-time mothers usually efface the cervix completely before it dilates much
options.D: Multiparas complete all cervical dilatation before any effacement starts

explanation: In first-time mothers, the cervix typically thins out entirely first, whereas women who have given birth before often undergo effacement and dilatation at the same time. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h5)

question: Which gland releases oxytocin into the bloodstream when the cervix stretches during labor?

options.A: Thyroid gland
options.B: Posterior pituitary gland
options.C: Adrenal cortex gland
options.D: Anterior pituitary gland

explanation: Nerve impulses from the stretched cervix signal the brain, which causes the posterior pituitary gland to release stored oxytocin. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h6)

question: Why is Ferguson's reflex considered a positive feedback loop?

options.A: Oxytocin production immediately stops the moment the cervix begins to dilate
options.B: Prostaglandins neutralize the hormones that cause the uterus to contract
options.C: Contractions cause cervical stretch, which releases more oxytocin to increase contractions
options.D: The mother's blood pressure drops to slow down the labor process

explanation: Positive feedback loops amplify the response, meaning stretching leads to oxytocin release, which causes stronger contractions and more stretching. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is a normal contraction frequency during active first-stage labor?

options.A: Three to five contractions every ten minutes
options.B: One to two contractions every twenty minutes
options.C: Continuous cramping with no resting phase
options.D: Eight to ten contractions every five minutes

explanation: An effective active labor pattern typically consists of 3 to 5 contractions in a 10-minute window, leaving enough time for uterine relaxation and blood flow to the baby. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h7)

question: A midwife assesses a laboring woman and notices contractions lasting 60 seconds every 2 minutes with no resting time between them. What is the main concern here?

options.A: Exhaustion of the maternal posterior pituitary gland
options.B: Reduced blood flow and oxygen supply to the fetus
options.C: Premature rupture of the fetal membranes
options.D: Rapid cervical dilatation exceeding ten centimeters

explanation: Without a resting break between contractions, uterine blood vessels stay squeezed shut, cutting off oxygen exchange and risking fetal distress. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T3#BMP212_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is the most common and favorable position for a baby's head during a normal head-first (cephalic) birth?

options.A: Occipito-posterior position
options.B: Mento-anterior position
options.C: Sacro-posterior position
options.D: Occipito-anterior position

explanation: In the occipito-anterior position, the baby's head faces backward toward the mother's spine, fitting smoothly through the widest parts of the pelvis for an efficient delivery. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T4#BMP212_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why does a baby's head make automatic twisting and turning movements as it travels down the birth canal?

options.A: Uterine contractions push the fetus down against resistance from the pelvic floor.
options.B: The mother actively pushes the baby in different directions using her abdominal muscles.
options.C: Midwives manually rotate the baby's head during routine vaginal examinations.
options.D: The fetus deliberately adjusts its body to find a more comfortable position.

explanation: As the uterus contracts and pushes the baby downward, the sloping bones and muscles of the pelvis act like a slide, forcing the head to passively turn and find the easiest path. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T4#BMP212_U2_T4_h1)

question: What is the term for the overlapping of the baby's skull bones so the head can fit through the birth canal?

options.A: Descent
options.B: Restitution
options.C: Flexion
options.D: Molding

explanation: Molding allows the flexible plates of the baby's skull to overlap slightly, temporarily changing the head shape to safely ease passage through the pelvis. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T4#BMP212_U2_T4_h2)

question: A first-time mother has a narrow pelvic inlet and a larger baby. Which core element of normal labor is facing a challenge here?

options.A: The passenger
options.B: The placenta
options.C: The power
options.D: The passage

explanation: The maternal bony pelvis represents the passage through which the baby must travel. A narrow inlet directly impacts this passage. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T4#BMP212_U2_T4_h2)

question: Which movement happens when the baby tucks its chin tightly against its chest?

options.A: Restitution
options.B: Flexion
options.C: Extension
options.D: Descent

explanation: Flexion forces the chin to the chest, allowing the baby to present the smallest possible head diameter to the birth canal. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T4#BMP212_U2_T4_h3)

question: What happens during the movement called restitution?

options.A: The fetal head untwists to align with its shoulders after delivery.
options.B: The baby's chin moves away from its chest as the head crowns.
options.C: The widest diameter of the fetal head passes through the pelvic inlet.
options.D: The anterior shoulder slips out from beneath the pubic bone.

explanation: Restitution is the quick, natural untwisting of the baby's head just outside the vagina, bringing it back into a straight line with the shoulders. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T4#BMP212_U2_T4_h3)

question: Which transverse diameter of the fetal head must pass through the pelvic inlet for engagement to happen?

options.A: Biparietal diameter
options.B: Occipito-frontal diameter
options.C: Suboccipito-bregmatic diameter
options.D: Mentovertical diameter

explanation: Engagement is confirmed when the widest side-to-side measurement of the baby's head, the biparietal diameter, successfully enters the pelvic inlet. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T4#BMP212_U2_T4_h4)

question: What maternal pelvic landmarks do midwives use to check the station (descent) of the baby's head?

options.A: Iliac crests
options.B: Ischial spines
options.C: Sacral promontory
options.D: Pubic symphysis

explanation: The ischial spines act as the zero reference point (station 0) to measure how far down the baby's head has traveled into the pelvis. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T4#BMP212_U2_T4_h4)

question: Why is head flexion so important for the baby during labor?

options.A: It prevents the umbilical cord from slipping past the presenting part.
options.B: It ensures the baby's shoulders rotate inside the pelvic cavity.
options.C: It replaces a larger head diameter with a smaller one to ease passage.
options.D: It stops the mother from feeling premature urges to push.

explanation: By tucking the chin, the baby swaps a wide head measurement for a much smaller one, making it much easier to slide through the pelvis. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T4#BMP212_U2_T4_h5)

question: Which part of the mother's body causes the baby's head to turn internally?

options.A: Pubic symphysis
options.B: Pelvic floor muscles
options.C: Cervical os
options.D: Sacral promontory

explanation: The sloping muscles of the pelvic floor act like a smooth slide, guiding the back of the baby's head to rotate forward toward the pubic bone. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T4#BMP212_U2_T4_h5)

question: What acts as the pivot point around which the baby's head lifts during extension?

options.A: Ischial spine
options.B: Coccyx tip
options.C: Pubic symphysis
options.D: Sacral promontory

explanation: The lower edge of the pubic symphysis acts as a hinge, allowing the baby's head to pivot upward and emerge from the vagina. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T4#BMP212_U2_T4_h6)

question: What causes the baby's head to untwist (restitution) right after it is born?

options.A: The shoulders inside the pelvis rotate to match the delivered head.
options.B: The midwife gently twists the head to help deliver the shoulders.
options.C: The head untwists to relieve the twist created during internal rotation.
options.D: Contractions of the abdominal wall force the neck bones to straighten.

explanation: Restitution happens naturally because the neck uncoils, letting the head snap back into alignment with the shoulders inside. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T4#BMP212_U2_T4_h6)

question: Which of the baby's shoulders usually delivers first?

options.A: Left shoulder
options.B: Right shoulder
options.C: Posterior shoulder
options.D: Anterior shoulder

explanation: The front shoulder (anterior shoulder) slips out from right under the pubic arch first, before the back shoulder follows over the perineum. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T4#BMP212_U2_T4_h7)

question: Why does the baby's head make another visible turn (external rotation) shortly after birth?

options.A: Maternal pushing forces the neck muscles to contract.
options.B: The midwife turns the head to prevent shoulder dystocia.
options.C: The shoulders rotate internally inside the pelvis to fit the outlet.
options.D: The baby turns its face to breathe fresh air after birth.

explanation: As the shoulders inside the pelvis turn to line up for delivery, that internal movement makes the head outside turn along with them. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T4#BMP212_U2_T4_h7)

question: What chart do midwives use daily to record and track the progress of labor?

options.A: Pelvimeter
options.B: Cardiotocograph
options.C: Ultrasound scanner
options.D: Partograph

explanation: The partograph is a standardized visual chart used to track cervical dilation, baby's descent, and the overall well-being of mother and baby. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T4#BMP212_U2_T4_h8)

question: During a vaginal exam, a midwife notices the baby's head is not flexing or turning as expected. Why is writing this down immediately so important?

options.A: To detect abnormal progress and intervene before complications arise.
options.B: To prevent the need for any further vaginal examinations.
options.C: To calculate the exact birth weight of the baby before delivery.
options.D: To prove that the mother is not pushing hard enough during contractions.

explanation: Catching labor delays or unusual positioning early helps the midwife take action before the mother or baby faces serious distress. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T4#BMP212_U2_T4_h8)

question: How often should you check a laboring woman's temperature after her water has broken?

options.A: Every two hours
options.B: Once every shift
options.C: Every four hours
options.D: Every six hours

explanation: When membranes rupture, the risk of infection goes up. Checking the temperature every two hours helps catch any early signs of fever. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T5#BMP212_U2_T5_h1)

question: A woman's water breaks spontaneously during active labor. What is the most important monitoring adjustment to make?

options.A: Increase the frequency of maternal temperature checks
options.B: Check maternal blood pressure only once every six hours
options.C: Delay listening to the baby's heartbeat until the pushing stage begins
options.D: Stop recording maternal pulse and focus entirely on contractions

explanation: Ruptured membranes mean a higher chance of infection, so checking the mother's temperature more often allows you to spot early signs of chorioamnionitis. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T5#BMP212_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why did traditional hospital policies require women to fast during the entire duration of labor?

options.A: Because the digestive system stops working completely
options.B: To reduce the frequency and intensity of uterine contractions
options.C: To prevent aspiration if general anesthesia became necessary
options.D: To speed up the overall progression of cervical dilation

explanation: Fasting was originally required to lower the risk of stomach contents entering the lungs if an emergency required putting the mother to sleep. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T5#BMP212_U2_T5_h2)

question: What is the main benefit of letting low-risk women in labor drink clear fluids or oral rehydration solutions?

options.A: Preventing maternal dehydration and ketosis
options.B: Lowering the resting blood pressure readings
options.C: Completely stopping all labor discomfort
options.D: Accelerating fetal descent through the pelvis

explanation: Labor takes a lot of energy. Drinking fluids keeps the mother hydrated and prevents her body from breaking down fat into ketones. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T5#BMP212_U2_T5_h2)

question: Which part of the spinal cord receives the main pain signals from contractions during the first stage of labor?

options.A: C1 to C5
options.B: T10 to L1
options.C: S2 to S4
options.D: L4 to S1

explanation: Nerve fibers carrying pain signals from the uterus and cervix enter the spinal cord between the tenth thoracic and first lumbar vertebrae. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T5#BMP212_U2_T5_h3)

question: How does severe anxiety and fear directly affect the physical progress of labor?

options.A: It automatically forces the cervix to dilate twice as fast
options.B: It increases the production of natural pain-relieving endorphins
options.C: It blocks all pain sensations from reaching the brain
options.D: It releases hormones like adrenaline that can slow down contractions

explanation: High stress triggers the release of catecholamines, which can reduce blood flow to the uterus and make labor take longer. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T5#BMP212_U2_T5_h3)

question: Which comfort measure helps relieve lower back pain when a baby is lying in a posterior position?

options.A: Inhalation of pure oxygen
options.B: Lying flat on the back
options.C: Restricted fluid intake
options.D: Sacral counterpressure

explanation: Applying firm, steady pressure to the lower back helps ease the intense back pressure felt when the baby's head is posterior. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T5#BMP212_U2_T5_h4)

question: A woman in early labor is having strong cramps and feels very tense. What is the best first step to take?

options.A: Administering intravenous general anesthesia
options.B: Encouraging upright positioning and movement
options.C: Applying immediate absolute bedrest restrictions
options.D: Insisting she lies completely flat on her back

explanation: Staying upright and moving around are simple, natural ways to help manage early labor discomfort while letting gravity assist. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T5#BMP212_U2_T5_h4)

question: What is a major risk of giving systemic opioid pain relief to a woman who is very close to giving birth?

options.A: Complete stoppage of breast milk
options.B: Sudden high blood pressure spikes
options.C: Neonatal respiratory depression
options.D: Permanent paralysis of the legs

explanation: Opioids cross the placenta. If birth happens shortly after the injection, the newborn may have trouble breathing on its own. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T5#BMP212_U2_T5_h5)

question: Why is regular blood pressure monitoring so important after a woman receives an epidural?

options.A: High blood pressure is required to make the spinal medication work properly
options.B: Epidurals can cause blood vessels to relax, leading to maternal low blood pressure
options.C: The medication stops the heart from beating if checked less than hourly
options.D: It helps the midwife calculate the exact minute of cervical full dilation

explanation: Epidural anesthesia can block sympathetic nerves and lower blood pressure, which might reduce oxygen flow to the baby if not caught early. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T5#BMP212_U2_T5_h5)

question: What is the primary tool used in Nigerian maternity units to track labor progress and vital signs visually?

options.A: The daily dietary menu
options.B: The pediatric growth chart
options.C: The surgical audit log
options.D: The partograph

explanation: The partograph is a standard chart used to record vital signs, cervical dilation, and labor progress all in one place. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T5#BMP212_U2_T5_h6)

question: Why must you evaluate and document whether a pain relief method actually worked?

options.A: To confirm whether the method helped the mother cope with contractions
options.B: To ensure the patient stays asleep until the second stage begins
options.C: To replace the need for charting vital signs on the partograph
options.D: To prove that medication costs can be billed at a higher rate

explanation: Documenting the response lets you know if the current pain relief is working or if you need to try a different approach to support the mother. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T5#BMP212_U2_T5_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of using a partograph during labor?

options.A: To replace the need for physical abdominal examinations
options.B: To provide an early visual warning when labor becomes abnormal
options.C: To record only the medications given after delivery
options.D: To calculate the exact date and time of conception

explanation: The partograph is designed as a graphical tool to track labor progress and give early signals if something is going wrong. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T6#BMP212_U2_T6_h1)

question: Why is the partograph particularly valuable in busy healthcare facilities?

options.A: It removes the requirement to monitor the fetal heart rate
options.B: It acts as a clear communication tool between different shifts of staff
options.C: It completely automates the delivery process without human effort
options.D: It guarantees that no complications will ever happen during birth

explanation: A graphical chart allows incoming midwives to see at a glance how labor has progressed over time. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T6#BMP212_U2_T6_h1)

question: Which of the following parameters is NOT recorded in the fetal condition section of the partograph?

options.A: Fetal heart rate
options.B: Amniotic fluid status
options.C: Maternal blood pressure
options.D: Degree of skull molding

explanation: Maternal blood pressure belongs to the maternal condition section, while heart rate and liquor status belong to the fetal section. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T6#BMP212_U2_T6_h2)

question: Where on the partograph is the graphical tracking of cervical dilation recorded?

options.A: Progress of labor section
options.B: Maternal condition section
options.C: Summary of delivery section
options.D: Medications and fluids section

explanation: Cervical dilation and head descent are core measurements tracked under the progress of labor part of the chart. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T6#BMP212_U2_T6_h2)

question: At what centimeter of cervical dilatation does the alert line on the partograph traditionally begin?

options.A: 2 cm
options.B: 7 cm
options.C: 4 cm
options.D: 10 cm

explanation: The active phase of labor is recognized to start at 4 cm, which is where the alert line begins. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T6#BMP212_U2_T6_h3)

question: What is a key action when a woman's labor progress crosses to the right of the alert line?

options.A: Administer a massive dose of pain relief medication
options.B: Stop all monitoring because normal labor has now concluded
options.C: Perform an immediate emergency Cesarean section in the same room
options.D: Evaluate the cause of slow progress and prepare for potential transfer

explanation: Reaching the alert line warns of slow progress, prompting assessment and preparations for moving the patient if needed. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T6#BMP212_U2_T6_h3)

question: How many hours to the right of the alert line is the action line placed on the standard partograph?

options.A: 4 hours
options.B: 6 hours
options.C: 8 hours
options.D: 2 hours

explanation: The action line is positioned exactly four hours to the right of the alert line to allow a clear window for warning before decisive intervention is mandatory. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T6#BMP212_U2_T6_h4)

question: A laboring woman's cervical dilatation curve crosses the action line on her partograph. What does this indicate?

options.A: The partograph was filled out incorrectly and should be discarded
options.B: Immediate medical intervention or delivery decision is required
options.C: The baby will be born naturally within the next ten minutes
options.D: No action is needed as long as the mother feels comfortable

explanation: Crossing the action line means delay is significant and active medical management or surgical delivery must be initiated. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T6#BMP212_U2_T6_h4)

question: Why is delayed plotting on a partograph hours after examinations take place discouraged?

options.A: It changes the fetal heart rate to an abnormal rhythm
options.B: It makes the paper chart look untidy and difficult to read
options.C: It uses up too much ink in the clinic's ballpoint pens
options.D: It hides delayed labor progress and delays necessary life-saving interventions

explanation: Delayed entry masks real-time problems, meaning the alert and action lines will not give their timely warning. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T6#BMP212_U2_T6_h5)

question: When interpreting labor progress, why must the midwife observe fetal head descent together with cervical dilatation?

options.A: To confirm that the baby is actually moving down the birth canal despite dilation
options.B: To decide whether the mother needs an enema
options.C: To calculate the exact birth weight of the infant before delivery
options.D: To determine the blood type of the mother

explanation: A cervix can dilate while the head stays high, which is a major sign of cephalopelvic disproportion. [learn more](BMP212_U2_T6#BMP212_U2_T6_h5)

question: What cervical measurement tells us that the second stage of labor has officially started?

options.A: Ten centimeters
options.B: Eight centimeters
options.C: Six centimeters
options.D: Twelve centimeters

explanation: The second stage begins when the cervix is fully open at ten centimeters. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T1#BMP212_U3_T1_h1)

question: What main activity sets the second stage of labor apart from the first stage?

options.A: Rapid thinning of the cervix
options.B: Initial engagement of the fetal head
options.C: Active pushing and delivery of the baby
options.D: Separation and delivery of the placenta

explanation: The first stage focuses on opening the cervix, while the second stage centers on pushing the baby down and out. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T1#BMP212_U3_T1_h1)

question: Which hormone is mainly responsible for causing strong uterine contractions in the second stage?

options.A: Oxytocin
options.B: Progesterone
options.C: Estrogen
options.D: Prolactin

explanation: Oxytocin stimulates the muscle of the uterus to trigger and maintain powerful contractions. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T1#BMP212_U3_T1_h2)

question: How does Ferguson's reflex help a mother during the second stage of labor?

options.A: It numbs the area to decrease labor pain
options.B: It relaxes the abdominal muscles to reduce tiredness
options.C: It causes an involuntary urge to push when the baby presses low
options.D: It prevents heavy bleeding by contracting blood vessels

explanation: Pressure from the baby's head on the pelvic floor sends signals that release oxytocin and create a natural urge to bear down. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T1#BMP212_U3_T1_h2)

question: What does a bulging perineum during the second stage of labor tell us?

options.A: The placenta is starting to separate
options.B: The amniotic membranes have ruptured early
options.C: Extra fluid has gathered in the lower uterus
options.D: The cervix is fully open and the baby is moving down

explanation: As the baby's head moves deep into the pelvis, it presses directly against the perineum, causing it to bulge outward. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T1#BMP212_U3_T1_h3)

question: Which of the following physical changes is NOT typically seen as the baby moves down onto the pelvic floor?

options.A: The anal sphincter relaxes
options.B: The cervix goes back down to two centimeters
options.C: The perineum bulges
options.D: Bloody show appears

explanation: By the time these signs happen, the cervix is already fully open at ten centimeters and has pulled back completely over the baby's head. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T1#BMP212_U3_T1_h3)

question: What happens during the movement called flexion as the baby travels through the pelvis?

options.A: The baby's chin tucks tightly against its chest
options.B: The baby's head turns sideways to face the hip
options.C: The baby straightens its legs to add pushing force
options.D: The shoulders turn to fit the pelvic outlet

explanation: Flexion helps the smallest part of the baby's head lead the way through the birth canal. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T1#BMP212_U3_T1_h4)

question: Why must internal rotation happen during normal labor?

options.A: To let the placenta detach safely from the uterine wall
options.B: To help the baby line up with the widest part of the lower pelvis
options.C: To keep the umbilical cord away from the neck
options.D: To trigger the mother's body to release oxytocin

explanation: Internal rotation turns the baby's head so it can navigate the curves of the lower pelvis. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T1#BMP212_U3_T1_h4)

question: When is the best time to check the baby's heartbeat during the second stage of labor?

options.A: Only at the very beginning of pushing
options.B: Every ten minutes regardless of contractions
options.C: Immediately after a uterine contraction
options.D: While the mother is actively pushing

explanation: Checking the heartbeat right after a contraction helps catch any drops in oxygen caused by labor stress. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T1#BMP212_U3_T1_h5)

question: A midwife sees thick green meconium in the amniotic fluid as the baby's head crowns. What is the most important first step?

options.A: Give oral oxytocin to speed up the birth
options.B: Ask the mother to stop pushing and rest for two hours
options.C: Get equipment and team ready for possible newborn resuscitation
options.D: Do an immediate instrumental delivery before checking vitals

explanation: Thick meconium can mean the baby experienced stress and might breathe in fluid, so being ready to care for the newborn right away is essential. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T1#BMP212_U3_T1_h5)

question: What clinical milestone marks the exact beginning of the second stage of labor?

options.A: Regular painful contractions
options.B: The rupture of membranes
options.C: Full cervical dilatation
options.D: The appearance of bloody show

explanation: The second stage officially starts when the cervix reaches complete ten centimeters dilatation, allowing the fetus to descend into the birth canal. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T2#BMP212_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why is clear communication with the mother important during labor preparation?

options.A: It stops the baby from moving too quickly
options.B: It helps reduce her anxiety and secures her active pushing
options.C: It prevents the need for an episiotomy entirely
options.D: It speeds up the natural dilation of the cervix

explanation: Explaining procedures lowers fear and helps the mother coordinate her breathing and pushing efforts effectively. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T2#BMP212_U3_T2_h1)

question: Which of these is NOT a recommended reason for performing an episiotomy?

options.A: Fetal distress requiring quick delivery
options.B: Persistent non-vertex malposition
options.C: Routine use in all first-time mothers
options.D: Anticipated shoulder dystocia

explanation: Current evidence shows routine episiotomy does not protect the perineum and should only be done for clear clinical indications. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T2#BMP212_U3_T2_h2)

question: A midwife supports the mother's perineum with sterile gauze and controls the speed of the baby's head as it crowns. What is the main goal of this practice?

options.A: To prevent severe perineal tearing
options.B: To speed up the second stage of labor
options.C: To stop the baby from breathing too early
options.D: To measure the exact weight of the infant

explanation: Controlled delivery of the head gives the perineal tissues time to stretch, reducing the risk of deep lacerations. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T2#BMP212_U3_T2_h2)

question: What movement does the fetal head normally make immediately after it is born outside the vagina?

options.A: Internal rotation
options.B: Extension
options.C: Restitution
options.D: Descent

explanation: After the head is delivered, it untwists and aligns back with the shoulders in a movement called restitution. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T2#BMP212_U3_T2_h3)

question: What immediate action should a midwife take if a loose nuchal cord is found around the baby's neck?

options.A: Pull hard on the shoulders to unwrap the cord
options.B: Gently slip the cord over the baby's head
options.C: Clamp and cut the cord immediately before the head is fully out
options.D: Push the baby back inside the uterus until the cord falls off

explanation: A loose cord can usually be looped over the fetal head without cutting it, provided there is enough slack. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T2#BMP212_U3_T2_h3)

question: Which shoulder is normally delivered first during a normal vaginal birth?

options.A: The posterior shoulder
options.B: Whichever shoulder is closest to the sacrum
options.C: The anterior shoulder
options.D: Both shoulders deliver at the exact same time

explanation: Gentle downward traction brings the anterior shoulder out from beneath the pubic bone first. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T2#BMP212_U3_T2_h4)

question: How should the midwife hold the baby's head while assisting the delivery of the shoulders?

options.A: With both hands placed over the parietal bones on the sides of the head
options.B: Using a pair of sterile obstetric forceps
options.C: By placing fingers directly inside the baby's mouth
options.D: By firmly grabbing the baby's neck and chin

explanation: Holding the head on the sides prevents excessive twisting of the neck and protects the cervical spine. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T2#BMP212_U3_T2_h4)

question: What is the primary reason for drying the newborn immediately with a warm towel?

options.A: To prevent heat loss through evaporation
options.B: To remove all vernix caseosa from the skin
options.C: To stimulate the baby to start crying loudly
options.D: To check the baby for birth marks and rashes

explanation: Wet skin causes rapid cooling through evaporation, so drying and wrapping the baby protects against hypothermia. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T2#BMP212_U3_T2_h5)

question: A midwife delivers a baby and places it on the mother's bare chest. What crucial check must the midwife perform on the mother before giving uterotonic medications?

options.A: Check if the placenta has already detached
options.B: Check if the mother wants to eat food
options.C: Check the abdomen to rule out another baby
options.D: Check the mother's blood pressure with a cuff

explanation: Palpating the abdomen ensures a twin pregnancy is not missed before giving oxytocin to expel the placenta. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T2#BMP212_U3_T2_h5)

question: What is the very first action a midwife should take immediately after a baby is born?

options.A: Weigh the infant on the delivery scale
options.B: Administer the vitamin K injection
options.C: Check if the baby is breathing or crying
options.D: Clamp and cut the umbilical cord instantly

explanation: Evaluating breathing and crying tells the midwife right away if the baby is transitioning smoothly or needs resuscitation. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T3#BMP212_U3_T3_h1)

question: Why is drying the newborn with a warm towel a critical priority right after delivery?

options.A: To stimulate the baby's digestive system
options.B: To prevent rapid heat loss from evaporation
options.C: To check for birth marks on the skin
options.D: To remove all traces of vernix caseosa

explanation: Wet skin causes rapid cooling through evaporation, making immediate drying essential to protect the newborn from cold stress. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T3#BMP212_U3_T3_h1)

question: Which of the following describes the correct approach to airway clearance for a vigorous newborn?

options.A: Routine deep suctioning of the mouth and nose
options.B: Immediate mechanical suctioning of the trachea
options.C: Washing the upper airway with sterile water
options.D: No routine suctioning if the baby is crying well

explanation: Healthy, vigorous babies clear their own airways naturally and do not need routine bulb suctioning. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T3#BMP212_U3_T3_h2)

question: Why is routine suctioning discouraged for healthy newborns?

options.A: It wastes valuable time needed for vitamin K administration
options.B: It makes the baby's skin too dry for identification tags
options.C: It permanently damages the delicate nasal mucosa
options.D: It can cause laryngeal spasm or slow the heart rate

explanation: Unnecessary suctioning stimulates the vagus nerve, which can dangerously lower the heart rate and cause breathing spasms. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T3#BMP212_U3_T3_h2)

question: How many blood vessels should a midwife normally see when inspecting the cut surface of the umbilical cord?

options.A: Three arteries and two veins
options.B: One large artery and one vein
options.C: Two arteries and one vein
options.D: Two veins and one artery

explanation: A normal umbilical cord contains three vessels, consisting of a pair of arteries carrying deoxygenated blood and a single vein carrying oxygenated blood. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T3#BMP212_U3_T3_h3)

question: What is the primary benefit of delaying cord clamping for a few minutes after birth?

options.A: It prevents the mother from experiencing severe hemorrhage
options.B: It allows the placenta to expel much faster
options.C: It makes the newborn's skin less slippery to hold
options.D: It improves infant iron stores and reduces anemia

explanation: Waiting to clamp the cord allows extra blood to flow from the placenta to the baby, building up iron reserves for the first months of life. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T3#BMP212_U3_T3_h3)

question: At what specific time intervals is the Apgar score routinely assessed after birth?

options.A: At 1 and 5 minutes
options.B: At 5 and 10 minutes
options.C: At 10 and 20 minutes
options.D: At birth and 30 minutes

explanation: The standard Apgar assessment takes place at one minute to gauge tolerance of labor and at five minutes to measure extrauterine adaptation. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T3#BMP212_U3_T3_h4)

question: A newborn has a strong heart rate, pink body with blue hands and feet, active movement, and a good cry. What is the Apgar score?
explanation: A heart rate over 100 scores 2, pink body with blue extremities scores 1, active movement scores 2, and a good cry scores 2. This totals 9 because of the 1 point deduction for peripheral cyanosis. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T3#BMP212_U3_T3_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the primary mechanisms of heat loss in a newborn?

options.A: Conduction
options.B: Evaporation
options.C: Transpiration
options.D: Radiation

explanation: The four main mechanisms of neonatal heat loss are conduction, convection, radiation, and evaporation. Transpiration is a plant process. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T3#BMP212_U3_T3_h5)

question: Why is keeping a newborn warm so important for their immediate metabolic health?

options.A: Chilly babies are unable to produce any tears when crying
options.B: Cold skin prevents the Apgar score from reaching 10
options.C: Cold stress can lead to metabolic acidosis and hypoglycemia
options.D: Low body temperature stops the umbilical cord from clotting

explanation: When a baby gets cold, the body burns brown fat to generate heat, consuming oxygen and glucose rapidly, which triggers dangerous acid buildup and low blood sugar. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T3#BMP212_U3_T3_h5)

question: What crucial detail must be recorded alongside the baby's weight and gender in the delivery register?

options.A: Type of labor bed used
options.B: Father's occupation
options.C: Exact time of birth
options.D: Mother's blood group

explanation: The exact time of birth is a legal and clinical necessity needed for tracking medication schedules, pediatric assessments, and developmental milestones. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T3#BMP212_U3_T3_h6)

question: What is the main purpose of giving a structured handover to the postnatal ward staff?

options.A: To clear the delivery room for the next incoming mother
options.B: To verify that all hospital equipment has been returned
options.C: To hand over legal responsibility for the delivery documentation
options.D: To ensure continuity of observation and patient safety

explanation: A structured handover communicates important risk factors and care details so the postnatal team can monitor the mother and baby safely. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T3#BMP212_U3_T3_h6)

question: When does the third stage of labor officially begin?

options.A: After the complete delivery of the baby
options.B: When the mother feels the urge to push
options.C: At the start of full cervical dilation
options.D: When the placenta starts to separate

explanation: The third stage starts right after the baby is fully born and ends when the placenta and membranes come out. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T4#BMP212_U3_T4_h1)

question: What makes the third stage of labor a time that requires close watch by the midwife?

options.A: There is a high risk of heavy bleeding
options.B: Infection rates peak immediately after birth
options.C: The mother is too exhausted to breathe well
options.D: The cervix usually tears during this time

explanation: Because the placental site leaves open blood vessels, postpartum hemorrhage is the main danger during this brief stage. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T4#BMP212_U3_T4_h1)

question: Which placental separation pattern begins at the center and looks like an inverted umbrella upon delivery?

options.A: Cotyledonary separation
options.B: Duncan mechanism
options.C: Schultze mechanism
options.D: Decidual detachment

explanation: The Schultze mechanism starts centrally, forming a clot that turns the placenta inside out as it exits. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T4#BMP212_U3_T4_h2)

question: What causes the placenta to peel away from the uterine wall right after the baby is born?

options.A: The sudden rush of amniotic fluid pushing it down
options.B: The continuous pumping action of the fetal heart
options.C: The forceful pulling of the umbilical cord by the attendant
options.D: The sudden reduction in the surface area of the uterus

explanation: When the uterus shrinks rapidly after birth, the rigid placenta cannot shrink with it, causing it to tear away. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T4#BMP212_U3_T4_h2)

question: Which of these is NOT a sign that the placenta has separated?

options.A: Continuous severe lower abdominal pain
options.B: A sudden gush of dark blood from the vagina
options.C: Lengthening of the visible umbilical cord
options.D: The uterus changing to a globular shape

explanation: Severe continuous pain is a sign of complications like abruption or rupture, not normal physiological placental separation. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T4#BMP212_U3_T4_h3)

question: A midwife notices that the umbilical cord hanging from the vagina has suddenly grown longer and the uterus is globular. What do these signs tell her?

options.A: The bladder is completely empty
options.B: The placenta has separated and moved down
options.C: The baby has not been fully delivered yet
options.D: A postpartum hemorrhage has already begun

explanation: Cord lengthening and a globular uterine shape are classic indicators that the placenta has detached and descended. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T4#BMP212_U3_T4_h3)

question: What main body action stops bleeding from the open vessels where the placenta was attached?

options.A: Rapid activation of systemic platelets and clotting factors
options.B: Natural cooling of the uterus from amniotic fluid loss
options.C: Contraction of crisscrossing myometrial muscle fibers
options.D: Pressure from the baby pressing on the cervix

explanation: The myometrium acts as living ligatures, squeezing the blood vessels shut to control bleeding after birth. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T4#BMP212_U3_T4_h4)

question: Why are blood clotting factors alone not enough to stop bleeding in the third stage of labor?

options.A: Pregnancy temporarily destroys all circulating clotting proteins
options.B: Clotting only works in arteries, not in the venous sinuses
options.C: The placenta prevents any clotting from happening inside the uterus
options.D: The vessels feeding the placenta are large and require muscular compression to close

explanation: Blood clots alone cannot withstand the high flow from large uterine vessels without the mechanical clamping of muscle fibers. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T4#BMP212_U3_T4_h4)

question: What defines the physiological method of placental expulsion?

options.A: Applying steady downward traction on the cord without waiting
options.B: Using manual removal of the placenta under regional anesthesia
options.C: Using natural maternal effort and gravity without drugs or pulling
options.D: Injecting oxytocin immediately after the baby's shoulder is born

explanation: Physiological management lets the body expel the placenta completely on its own without medical or physical interference. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T4#BMP212_U3_T4_h5)

question: What is the main benefit of active management of the third stage compared to physiological management?

options.A: It entirely eliminates the need for any midwife supervision
options.B: It significantly reduces the risk of postpartum hemorrhage
options.C: It prevents all perineal tears from occurring
options.D: It makes the delivery of the baby happen much faster

explanation: Active management uses uterotonics and controlled traction to shorten the third stage and lower blood loss. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T4#BMP212_U3_T4_h5)

question: When does the third stage of labor officially begin?

options.A: As soon as the amniotic sac ruptures
options.B: Right after the baby is born
options.C: When the mother feels contraction pains
options.D: When the placenta starts to separate

explanation: The third stage runs from the moment the baby is fully born until the placenta and membranes are safely delivered. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T5#BMP212_U3_T5_h1)

question: What is the main reason for performing Active Management of the Third Stage of Labor (AMTSL)?

options.A: To prevent heavy postpartum bleeding
options.B: To shorten the second stage of labor
options.C: To speed up the healing of perineal tears
options.D: To help the baby breathe much better

explanation: The main goal of AMTSL is to prevent primary postpartum hemorrhage by helping the uterus contract and delivering the placenta safely. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T5#BMP212_U3_T5_h1)

question: Which drug is the safest and most effective first choice for routine AMTSL?

options.A: Misoprostol
options.B: Magnesium sulfate
options.C: Ergometrine
options.D: Oxytocin

explanation: Oxytocin is preferred because it works quickly and has very few side effects for healthy mothers. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T5#BMP212_U3_T5_h2)

question: Why must ergometrine be avoided when managing a mother with severe high blood pressure?

options.A: It takes too many hours to start working
options.B: It makes the placenta stick to the uterine wall
options.C: It stops breast milk production completely
options.D: It can cause dangerous spikes in blood pressure

explanation: Ergometrine tightens blood vessels across the body, which can dangerously raise blood pressure in women who already have hypertension. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T5#BMP212_U3_T5_h2)

question: During controlled cord traction, why does the midwife place one hand on the mother's lower abdomen?

options.A: To apply counter-pressure and prevent uterine inversion
options.B: To squeeze blood out of the umbilical cord vessels
options.C: To check if there is a second baby hiding inside
options.D: To push the baby's shoulders out of the birth canal

explanation: Abdominal counter-pressure supports the lower uterus, keeping it in place while the cord is gently pulled. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T5#BMP212_U3_T5_h3)

question: A midwife is waiting to perform controlled cord traction. What clinical sign must she check for first?

options.A: The total cessation of all maternal postpartum shivering
options.B: Complete relaxation of the mother's abdominal wall
options.C: An increase in the mother's pulse rate above 100
options.D: Signs of placental separation and a contracted uterus

explanation: Controlled cord traction is only done after confirming the uterus is contracted and the placenta has separated, which prevents cord snapping and heavy bleeding. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T5#BMP212_U3_T5_h3)

question: What does a soft, boggy uterus indicate right after the placenta is delivered?

options.A: Bladder distension
options.B: Perineal hematoma
options.C: Uterine atony
options.D: Retained membranes

explanation: A soft or boggy uterus means the muscle fibers have not contracted firmly, which is known as uterine atony. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T5#BMP212_U3_T5_h4)

question: How often should a midwife check the tone of the uterus during the first hour after birth?

options.A: Once every hour
options.B: Only when bleeding starts
options.C: Every 15 minutes
options.D: Every 30 minutes

explanation: Checking the uterus every 15 minutes during the first hour helps catch relaxation early before heavy bleeding starts. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T5#BMP212_U3_T5_h4)

question: What is the main risk if a midwife waits to give the uterotonic drug until after the placenta comes out?

options.A: Severe spasm of the cervix trapping remaining blood clots
options.B: Permanent damage to the nerves inside the birth canal
options.C: Immediate infection of the raw internal uterine cavity
options.D: Increased risk of postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony

explanation: Giving the drug early helps the uterus contract before bleeding can start, preventing atonic postpartum hemorrhage. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T5#BMP212_U3_T5_h5)

question: What danger happens if a student midwife pulls on the umbilical cord right after the baby is born, before giving any drugs?

options.A: Complete failure of the milk-letdown reflex
options.B: Cord snapping, retained placenta, or uterine inversion
options.C: Spontaneous rupture of the mother's urinary bladder
options.D: Delayed breathing adaptation in the newborn baby

explanation: Pulling on the cord before the uterus is contracted and before drugs take effect can snap the cord or pull the uterus inside out. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T5#BMP212_U3_T5_h5)

question: After how many minutes without delivery should a midwife suspect a retained placenta during AMTSL?

options.A: 10 minutes
options.B: 30 minutes
options.C: 5 minutes
options.D: 60 minutes

explanation: If the placenta does not deliver within 30 minutes despite AMTSL, clinical guidelines require action for a retained placenta. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T5#BMP212_U3_T5_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a required detail when documenting the third stage of labor?

options.A: The estimated blood loss volume
options.B: The baby's birth weight in grams
options.C: The completeness of the placenta
options.D: The time the uterotonic was given

explanation: While birth weight is important newborn information, it is recorded separately from the third-stage summary of drug timing, blood loss, and placental delivery. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T5#BMP212_U3_T5_h6)

question: What is the main physical sign the midwife checks right after the third stage of labor ends?

options.A: A hard, well-contracted uterus
options.B: A high-riding floating fundus
options.C: A completely empty pelvic cavity
options.D: A soft and boggy lower segment

explanation: A firmly contracted uterus is vital right after delivery to clamp down on open blood vessels and prevent heavy bleeding. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T6#BMP212_U3_T6_h1)

question: Why is the placenta examined right after delivery instead of waiting until the mother is settled?

options.A: To preserve the tissue samples for routine laboratory culture
options.B: To prevent the cord vessels from collapsing completely
options.C: To quickly spot missing pieces that could cause bleeding
options.D: To measure the exact total weight for the baby's chart

explanation: Checking the placenta right away ensures no pieces are left inside the uterus, which can cause severe postpartum hemorrhage. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T6#BMP212_U3_T6_h1)

question: How should the midwife hold the placenta to inspect the fetal surface and membranes?

options.A: By the umbilical cord allowing membranes to hang
options.B: Flat on a stainless steel tray with the maternal side up
options.C: Submerged fully in a basin of warm sterile water
options.D: Rolled tightly into a cylinder from edge to edge

explanation: Holding the cord lets the delicate membranes drape downward so the midwife can easily check if they are complete and intact. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T6#BMP212_U3_T6_h2)

question: Which finding on the maternal side of the placenta needs immediate action?

options.A: A branching pattern of normal surface blood vessels
options.B: A slightly pale area near the center of the disc
options.C: A thin layer of dark blood clots loosely attached
options.D: A missing section of cotyledons leaving a raw gap

explanation: Missing cotyledons mean tissue remains inside the uterus, which requires medical attention to stop bleeding. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T6#BMP212_U3_T6_h2)

question: What is the normal number of blood vessels found in a healthy human umbilical cord?

options.A: Two vessels
options.B: Five vessels
options.C: Three vessels
options.D: Four vessels

explanation: A normal cord has two arteries and one vein, making a total of three vessels. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T6#BMP212_U3_T6_h3)

question: What does a two-vessel umbilical cord usually prompt the midwife to arrange for the newborn?

options.A: Intravenous fluid therapy to support circulation
options.B: Further physical checks for hidden birth defects
options.C: Emergency surgery to remove the remaining artery
options.D: Immediate placement in a neonatal intensive care incubator

explanation: A single umbilical artery can sometimes be linked to kidney or heart issues, so the baby needs a careful physical assessment. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T6#BMP212_U3_T6_h3)

question: Which degree of perineal tear involves injury to the anal sphincter muscles?

options.A: Third-degree tear
options.B: Fourth-degree tear
options.C: First-degree tear
options.D: Second-degree tear

explanation: A third-degree tear involves disruption of the anal sphincter muscles, whereas a fourth-degree tear also includes the rectal lining. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T6#BMP212_U3_T6_h4)

question: A woman has a firm uterus and steady bright red bleeding after delivery. What should the midwife check next?

options.A: The exact weight of the delivered placenta
options.B: The newborn baby for signs of birth asphyxia
options.C: The mother's blood pressure for sudden hypertension
options.D: The cervix and vagina for unmanaged lacerations

explanation: When the uterus is hard but bleeding continues, the source is usually an unrepaired tear in the birth canal, such as the cervix or vagina. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T6#BMP212_U3_T6_h4)

question: Why is a rectal examination sometimes done right after stitching a deep perineal tear?

options.A: To remove any remaining lochial discharge from the vault
options.B: To confirm no stitches accidentally entered the rectum
options.C: To stimulate normal bowel movements after the repair
options.D: To check the resting tone of the internal anal sphincter

explanation: A final check ensures stitches did not pass through the rectal wall, which helps prevent infection and other complications. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T6#BMP212_U3_T6_h5)

question: What is the main reason for closing a perineal wound in separate anatomical layers?

options.A: To prevent dead space and reduce the risk of blood pooling
options.B: To allow the outer skin stitches to dissolve much faster
options.C: To make the scar completely invisible within a few weeks
options.D: To increase the overall tightness of the pelvic floor muscles

explanation: Layered closure eliminates empty spaces where blood can collect and form painful clots, supporting proper healing. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T6#BMP212_U3_T6_h5)

question: What important detail about the placenta must be recorded in the delivery notes?

options.A: The total cost of the sterile instruments opened
options.B: Whether it was complete with all cotyledons present
options.C: The exact brand name of the delivery basin used
options.D: The specific room temperature during the third stage

explanation: Documenting placental completeness confirms that no retained tissue was left inside the uterus. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T6#BMP212_U3_T6_h6)

question: Why is accurate documentation of a perineal repair important in clinical practice?

options.A: It replaces the need to check the woman's vital signs
options.B: It guides ongoing care and tracks the healing progress
options.C: It is required primarily for hospital financial audits
options.D: It prevents the mother from feeling any postpartum pain

explanation: Detailed notes inform other health workers about the extent of trauma and the type of repair, guiding future assessments. [learn more](BMP212_U3_T6#BMP212_U3_T6_h6)

question: Roughly how many weeks does the normal puerperium period last?

options.A: Six weeks
options.B: Two weeks
options.C: Twelve weeks
options.D: Six months

explanation: The postnatal period spans approximately six weeks as the maternal organs return to their normal non-pregnant state. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T1#BMP212_U4_T1_h1)

question: What is the main purpose of the puerperium period?

options.A: Stimulating permanent weight gain
options.B: Reversing pregnancy-related bodily changes
options.C: Rapidly increasing maternal blood volume
options.D: Stopping all hormonal production

explanation: The main objective during this time is involution and systemic recovery back to the pre-pregnant baseline. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T1#BMP212_U4_T1_h1)

question: What uterine muscle action causes muscle fibers to stay shortened after each squeeze?

options.A: Hypertrophy
options.B: Retraction
options.C: Relaxation
options.D: Dilatation

explanation: Retraction allows muscle fibers to stay shortened after contracting, which steadily reduces uterine size and stops bleeding. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T1#BMP212_U4_T1_h2)

question: Why is efficient uterine muscle retraction right after placental delivery so important for the mother?

options.A: It prevents the expulsion of normal lochia discharge
options.B: It completely closes the external cervical os within hours
options.C: It compresses open blood vessels to prevent heavy bleeding
options.D: It accelerates the production of mature breast milk

explanation: Living sutures formed by retracted muscle fibers clamp down on torn placental vessels to stop postpartum hemorrhage. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T1#BMP212_U4_T1_h2)

question: What term describes the breakdown of excess uterine muscle tissue by internal enzymes after delivery?

options.A: Necrosis
options.B: Phagocytosis
options.C: Autolysis
options.D: Osmosis

explanation: Autolysis uses special enzymes to break down the heavy protein buildup inside enlarged muscle cells. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T1#BMP212_U4_T1_h3)

question: How does the body primarily handle the protein waste produced when uterine tissue breaks down?

options.A: Filtering the broken-down protein waste through the kidneys into urine
options.B: Reabsorbing the intact cells directly back into the arterial blood
options.C: Expelling all cellular debris exclusively through heavy sweating
options.D: Storing the waste permanently in lower abdominal fat

explanation: Proteins broken down during autolysis enter the bloodstream and are excreted by the kidneys, causing temporary postpartum diuresis. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T1#BMP212_U4_T1_h3)

question: At what average rate does the top of the uterus descend during the early postnatal days?

options.A: Five centimeters per day
options.B: One inch every two hours
options.C: One centimeter per day
options.D: Half a centimeter per week

explanation: Normal involution causes the fundus to drop roughly one fingerbreadth or centimeter daily until it enters the pelvic cavity. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T1#BMP212_U4_T1_h4)

question: On the tenth day after birth, a midwife finds the top of the uterus is still two fingers above the pubic bone. What does this finding most likely suggest?

options.A: Normal, accelerated recovery of the uterine tissues
options.B: An unusually small initial placental implantation site
options.C: Excessive fluid intake leading to bladder distension
options.D: Potential subinvolution or a retained placental fragment

explanation: By day ten, the uterus should normally have descended below the pelvic brim; failure to do so points toward subinvolution. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T1#BMP212_U4_T1_h4)

question: What is the expected color and consistency of lochia serosa during the middle of the first week after birth?

options.A: Dark green and foul-smelling
options.B: Bright red and thick
options.C: Pinkish-brown and watery
options.D: Yellowish-white and creamy

explanation: Lochia serosa appears between days four and ten, turning pinkish-brown as blood content decreases and serum increases. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T1#BMP212_U4_T1_h5)

question: What does a foul, offensive odor in the lochia discharge typically indicate?

options.A: Standard hormonal shifts following lactation
options.B: An active intrauterine or endometrial infection
options.C: Normal progress of physiological tissue breakdown
options.D: Rapid healing of a superficial perineal tear

explanation: A foul odor indicates bacterial multiplication within the uterine cavity, signaling potential postpartum sepsis. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T1#BMP212_U4_T1_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical way the body gets rid of extra pregnancy fluids in the early days after birth?

options.A: Heavy production of meconium stools
options.B: Elimination of plasma through lochial flow
options.C: Increased volume of clear urine output
options.D: Profuse sweating, especially at night

explanation: Postpartum fluid elimination occurs primarily through urinary diuresis and diaphoresis, not through excessive bowel movements. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T1#BMP212_U4_T1_h6)

question: How does the external opening of the cervix typically look after a woman has given birth vaginally compared to before her first pregnancy?

options.A: It remains tightly closed and permanently puckered like a drawstring
options.B: It disappears completely due to extensive postpartum scarring
options.C: It transforms from a small round opening into a transverse slit
options.D: It doubles in overall diameter while keeping a circular shape

explanation: The passage of the baby causes lateral tears in the cervix, healing into a characteristic transverse slit rather than a round opening. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T1#BMP212_U4_T1_h6)

question: Which hormone is primarily responsible for stimulating the growth and branching of the ductal system during pregnancy?

options.A: Oxytocin
options.B: Prolactin
options.C: Estrogen
options.D: Progesterone

explanation: Estrogen drives the development and branching of the milk ducts, while progesterone works on the alveolar glands. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T2#BMP212_U4_T2_h1)

question: What is the primary purpose of the oily secretions from the Montgomery glands on the areola?

options.A: Anchoring the baby's tongue during a feed
options.B: Lubricating and protecting the nipple
options.C: Providing extra protein to the baby
options.D: Stimulating the infant's rooting reflex

explanation: The Montgomery glands secrete a protective substance that keeps the nipple skin healthy and guards against cracking during frequent feeds. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T2#BMP212_U4_T2_h1)

question: Which hormone directly triggers the contraction of myoepithelial cells to cause the milk ejection reflex?

options.A: Prolactin
options.B: Progesterone
options.C: Human placental lactogen
options.D: Oxytocin

explanation: Oxytocin travels to the breast and causes the tiny muscles around the milk glands to squeeze milk into the ducts. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T2#BMP212_U4_T2_h2)

question: Why does milk production not happen in large amounts during pregnancy despite high prolactin levels?

options.A: High progesterone levels block prolactin's action
options.B: Estrogen destroys the prolactin receptors
options.C: The infant has not yet stimulated the nipple
options.D: The alveoli are not yet formed until birth

explanation: Circulating placental progesterone keeps milk production suppressed until the placenta is delivered at birth. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T2#BMP212_U4_T2_h2)

question: What is the primary immunological benefit of colostrum for a newborn baby?

options.A: Heavy concentration of iron stores
options.B: High percentage of saturated fats
options.C: Large amounts of simple carbohydrates
options.D: High concentration of secretory IgA

explanation: Colostrum is packed with antibodies like secretory IgA that line the baby's gut to prevent harmful germs from invading. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T2#BMP212_U4_T2_h3)

question: How does foremilk differ fundamentally from hindmilk within a single feed of mature milk?

options.A: Foremilk is higher in water content, while hindmilk is higher in fat content
options.B: Foremilk is produced at night, while hindmilk is produced during daylight feeds
options.C: Foremilk contains all the protein, while hindmilk contains only simple sugars
options.D: Foremilk is thick and yellow, while hindmilk is thin and clear

explanation: The milk at the start of a feed quenches thirst, while the milk at the end contains rich fats that satisfy the baby's hunger. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T2#BMP212_U4_T2_h3)

question: A postpartum mother complains of severe nipple pain and shows linear abrasions on her nipples. What is the most appropriate initial assessment to make?

options.A: Check the mother's temperature for signs of systemic infection
options.B: Prescribe an oral antifungal medication for suspected thrush
options.C: Advise the mother to stop breastfeeding for forty-eight hours
options.D: Observe the baby's latch and positioning at the breast

explanation: Nipple pain and trauma are almost always caused by poor attachment, making observation of the latch the essential first step. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T2#BMP212_U4_T2_h4)

question: Which visual sign indicates a correct, deep attachment during breastfeeding?

options.A: The mother feeling a sharp pinching sensation during sucking
options.B: The baby's cheeks appearing hollow and sucked inward
options.C: More areola visible above the baby's top lip than below
options.D: The baby's head turned to the side while the body faces upward

explanation: A deep latch requires taking a large mouthful of breast tissue from underneath, leaving more areola visible on top. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T2#BMP212_U4_T2_h4)

question: Which clinical feature helps distinguish mastitis from simple breast engorgement?

options.A: Leaking of colostrum between feeds
options.B: Tenderness when the baby begins to suck
options.C: Presence of bilateral breast swelling
options.D: Fever and systemic flu-like symptoms

explanation: Mastitis involves systemic signs like fever and chills, whereas engorgement and blocked ducts generally do not cause systemic illness. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T2#BMP212_U4_T2_h5)

question: Why is it important for a mother with mastitis to continue removing milk from the affected breast?

options.A: Breastmilk becomes toxic to the baby if it is allowed to stay in the gland
options.B: Stopping removal worsens stasis and increases the risk of abscess formation
options.C: Emptying the breast prevents the baby from catching the mother's infection
options.D: Prolactin levels will drop permanently if one feed is missed

explanation: Continuing to empty the breast prevents milk stasis from worsening and helps clear the infection alongside treatment. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T2#BMP212_U4_T2_h5)

question: Why is expressed breastmilk especially critical for the management of preterm infants in the neonatal unit?

options.A: Preterm infants cannot tolerate artificial milk formulas under any clinical circumstances
options.B: It provides specialized immunological protection and is easier for their immature gut to digest
options.C: It contains higher amounts of water to prevent dehydration caused by radiant warmers
options.D: Expressed milk eliminates the need for any vitamin or mineral supplementation

explanation: Preterm infants have fragile digestive systems and benefit immensely from the protective properties and easy digestibility of human milk. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T2#BMP212_U4_T2_h6)

question: What is the recommended initial action when a breastfeeding mother is prescribed a new medication?

options.A: Advise the mother to permanently wean her baby immediately
options.B: Switch the baby to full formula feeding without checking guidelines
options.C: Tell her to discard all expressed milk for the next two weeks
options.D: Consult a verified reference guide on drug safety during lactation

explanation: Most medications are safe during breastfeeding, so midwives must check reliable drug reference sources rather than automatically stopping breastfeeding. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T2#BMP212_U4_T2_h6)

question: How long does the puerperium period typically last?

options.A: Six months
options.B: Six weeks
options.C: Two weeks
options.D: Three months

explanation: The puerperium is defined as the six weeks following childbirth during which the body returns to its pre-pregnant state. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T3#BMP212_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why is structured postnatal care considered essential by midwives?

options.A: To catch complications early and support feeding
options.B: To hasten the return of menses within days
options.C: To guarantee the infant walks early
options.D: To eliminate the need for infant immunizations

explanation: Regular checks help midwives spot problems like bleeding or infection quickly while helping mothers feed successfully. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T3#BMP212_U4_T3_h1)

question: What is the primary reason for palpating the uterine fundus frequently on Day 1?

options.A: To measure the exact weight of the uterus
options.B: To stimulate early resumption of ovulation
options.C: To push out residual amniotic fluid
options.D: To ensure it is firm and contracted

explanation: A firm fundus means the uterine muscle fibers are clamping down on blood vessels, which stops postpartum bleeding. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T3#BMP212_U4_T3_h2)

question: A woman gave birth four hours ago and has not yet passed urine. What is the most appropriate initial action?

options.A: Encourage her to empty her bladder and monitor
options.B: Administer a strong intravenous diuretic
options.C: Insert an indwelling catheter immediately
options.D: Wait another twenty-four hours for spontaneous voiding

explanation: Prompt encouragement to void helps prevent bladder overdistension, which can push the uterus aside and cause heavy bleeding. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T3#BMP212_U4_T3_h2)

question: What color is the lochia discharge during the first few days after birth?

options.A: Whitish-yellow
options.B: Pinkish-brown
options.C: Dark green
options.D: Bright red

explanation: Lochia rubra consists mainly of blood and decidual tissue, making it bright red in the initial days postpartum. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T3#BMP212_U4_T3_h3)

question: Why does a midwife become concerned if lochia suddenly becomes foul-smelling two weeks after delivery?

options.A: It is a normal sign of rapid involution
options.B: It indicates the baby is not feeding well
options.C: It strongly suggests uterine infection
options.D: It means the mother is drinking too much water

explanation: Foul-smelling lochia combined with pelvic pain or fever points toward postpartum infection inside the uterus. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T3#BMP212_U4_T3_h3)

question: Around which days does milk volume typically increase, often leading to breast engorgement?

options.A: Week six
options.B: Days three to five
options.C: Day one
options.D: Days fourteen to twenty

explanation: Secretory activation, or milk coming in, usually happens around the third to fifth postnatal day. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T3#BMP212_U4_T3_h4)

question: What indicates a correct infant latch during breastfeeding?

options.A: Constant sharp pinching pain throughout the entire feed
options.B: A wide mouthful of breast tissue with the lower lip turned out
options.C: The infant's cheeks sucking inward into deep dimples
options.D: Only the tip of the nipple placed inside the baby's mouth

explanation: A deep latch protects the mother's skin from damage and allows the baby to effectively draw milk from the ducts. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T3#BMP212_U4_T3_h4)

question: Which condition typically resolves spontaneously within the first two weeks after birth without formal treatment?

options.A: Postpartum depression
options.B: Bipolar mania
options.C: Postpartum psychosis
options.D: Postpartum blues

explanation: The baby blues are very common, mild, and short-lived, clearing up on their own as hormones stabilize. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T3#BMP212_U4_T3_h5)

question: What distinguishes postpartum psychosis from postpartum blues?

options.A: Occurrence strictly on the very first day in the delivery ward
options.B: Physical breast pain caused by engorgement
options.C: Presence of severe symptoms like hallucinations and detachment from reality
options.D: Mild sadness that disappears after a single good night of sleep

explanation: Postpartum psychosis is a severe psychiatric emergency involving lost touch with reality, unlike the mild mood swings of the blues. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T3#BMP212_U4_T3_h5)

question: What is the maximum normal percentage of birth weight a term newborn may lose in the first few days?

options.A: Zero percent
options.B: Fifty percent
options.C: Twenty-five percent
options.D: Ten percent

explanation: An initial weight loss of up to ten percent is normal before feeding establishes and weight starts climbing again. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T3#BMP212_U4_T3_h6)

question: Why should a midwife advise parents to keep the umbilical cord stump dry?

options.A: To stop the baby from crying at night
options.B: To prevent the baby from passing meconium
options.C: To speed up the baby's growth in length
options.D: To encourage natural separation and prevent infection

explanation: Keeping the cord clean and dry helps it shrivel and fall off cleanly without bacterial growth setting in. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T3#BMP212_U4_T3_h6)

question: When does the final routine postnatal consultation usually take place?

options.A: At twenty-four hours postpartum
options.B: At six weeks postpartum
options.C: At six months postpartum
options.D: At two weeks postpartum

explanation: The six-week mark is the standard time for a final postnatal check to ensure full recovery and discuss family planning. [learn more](BMP212_U4_T3#BMP212_U4_T3_h7)

question: A breastfeeding mother asks if she needs contraception since her monthly period has not returned. What is the best midwifery response?

options.A: You only need contraception after your baby is weaned off milk
options.B: You are completely safe from pregnancy until your first menstrual flow
options.C: Breastfeeding prevents all pregnancies for the first full year
